explain.say: Three semicircular canals sit at right angles, like the floor and two walls of a room corner. When you turn your head, fluid inside lags behind and bends tiny hair cells, revealing the direction of the turn.

faq.a: They are three curved, fluid-filled tubes in the inner ear, set at right angles to each other. Each senses turning in one direction: nodding, shaking or tilting the head to the side.
asks: What do the loops in the inner ear do?

faq.q: How do we know which way is up?
faq.a: Two sacs in the inner ear contain tiny calcium carbonate crystals called otoliths resting on hair cells. Gravity pulls the crystals, bending the hairs, so the brain always knows which way is down.
asks: How does the ear sense gravity?

faq.q: Why do we have three semicircular canals?
faq.a: Space has three directions, so three canals at right angles can sense a turn in any direction. The brain combines their signals to work out exactly how the head is rotating.
asks: Why are there three loops in the ear?
Why are the canals at right angles?

faq.q: Does the cochlea help with balance?
faq.a: No, the cochlea is for hearing. It shares the same fluid system and nerve bundle as the balance organs, which is why they sit side by side in the inner ear.

faq.q: What does the balance nerve do?
faq.a: The balance nerve carries signals from the canals and sacs to the brainstem and cerebellum. The brain uses them to keep your eyes steady and your posture balanced, in a fraction of a second.
asks: How does the brain get balance signals?

facts: Each inner ear has three semicircular canals arranged roughly at right angles to one another.
The otoliths in the inner ear are tiny crystals of calcium carbonate.
